title: AI assistant for game designers on Mac: voice help in Figma and Notion, 2026
metaTitle: AI Assistant for Game Designers on Mac | Lazur
description: Lazur is a voice AI assistant for game designers on Mac. Hold a key to ask about your Figma or Notion screen and get answers out loud.
secondaryKeywords: AI for game design on Mac
intro: An AI assistant for game designers on a Mac should answer questions about the screen, not run your files. Lazur does the first part. Hold ⌥ ⌘ and it sees what you see, points at the thing you mean and answers out loud. It does not click for you, and it does not edit your design files.
tldr: Game designers lose much of the day to messages and file hunts. Most of the published figures come from general office research, not game studios.
Lazur points at layers in Figma, dictates into Notion, explains spreadsheet errors and drafts Slack replies.
Lazur does not click, edit or move anything in your files. You do the work.
Check your studio's NDA and AI rules before you show unreleased art or design.

blocks.text: Where a game designer's day goes

Most of a game designer's day is not design work. Microsoft surveyed 31,000 knowledge workers in 31 markets for its 2025 Work Trend Index. The average worker receives 117 emails a day and 153 Teams messages a weekday. Those figures cover office work in general, not game studios. Still, they sound like a normal Tuesday for many designers.

Microsoft also says employees are interrupted about every two minutes during core work hours. That adds up to 275 times a day, from meetings, emails or chats. Each interruption pulls you out of the feel of a combat loop or a progression curve. Getting back into that headspace often costs more than the interruption itself.

Asana's Anatomy of Work Index, published in 2021, looked at more than 13,000 knowledge workers. It found they spend almost two-thirds of their time on work about work. That phrase covers status updates, approvals, searching for files and chasing answers. Skilled work gets the rest. Asana is a vendor, so read the figure as a direction, not a precise split.

Some of this is a team habit, not a personal failure. A designer who answers every thread in order will lose the afternoon. The fix is not to ignore Slack. The fix is to cut the time each message takes and to keep your attention on the design for longer stretches.
What game industry AI use looks like in 2026

GDC's 2026 State of the Game Industry drew on responses from more than 2,300 game industry professionals. It found that 36% use generative AI tools as part of their job. Among daily uses, writing emails and code assistance were each cited by 47%. Prototyping came next at 35%. The mix shows where AI already helps game teams, and where it is still mostly email and code.

Those figures describe the whole industry, not game designers alone. No source here breaks out design work by role. Treat the numbers as context around your week. If you want your own split, keep a short log of where your time goes for a week. Then compare that log with these figures.
A Mac assistant for the desktop tools you already use

Most game design work happens in a few desktop apps. Figma handles interface and layout work, and FigJam covers whiteboard sessions. Some teams build prototypes in Unity. Figma's help center describes Figma Design as the tool for creating, sharing and testing designs for websites and apps. Its help pages do not mention games, so check the workflow on your own project.

The Figma desktop app supports macOS 12 (Monterey) or later. It runs on Intel and Apple silicon Macs and gives the same features as the browser version. A separate Figma Beta app runs next to the regular app. Check which one you open before you send a file link to the team.

blocks.text: Lazur runs alongside these apps. It is not a plugin or add-in for any of them, and it is not affiliated with any app maker. It listens and looks at the screen only while you hold the shortcut. It will not edit your file, move a layer or press a button for you.
What to ask Lazur, and the help you get back

Lazur has a few distinct modes, and the mode depends on what you ask. Asking where something is gets a circle and a label. Asking how to do something gets a guided walk through, one click at a time. Asking for text gets a draft or dictation. Pick the right mode and you save time.

items: Point: ask where something is. Lazur draws a circle and a label around it on your screen.
Explain: ask what a warning, message or formula means. Lazur answers out loud.
Guide: ask how to do something. Lazur walks you one click at a time and waits for each click.
Dictate: hold fn and speak. Clean, formatted text lands at the cursor in any app.
Draft: ask for a reply, a changelog line or a bug summary. You read it before you send it.
Research: send a question to Lazur's own Chrome tabs. It returns a summary and a report.
Everyday: timers, Apple Reminders, Calendar events, notes, music, volume, opening apps and links.

blocks.text: Figma: finding a HUD layer without the hunt

A HUD file grows fast. Health bars, ammo counters, minimap frames and pause menus pile up on one page. Finding one layer by scrolling the layers panel is slow. It also breaks your train of thought. It is a small cost that repeats all day.

Hold ⌥ ⌘ and ask: where is the stamina bar? Say the name you gave the layer, or describe it, such as the bottom left bar inside the HUD frame. Lazur draws a circle and a label where that layer sits, and says the answer out loud. Your hands stay on the mouse, and the file stays as it was.

Here is a worked example. You want to change how the stamina bar looks in the pause state. Ask Lazur to point at the stamina bar. Then ask it to guide you to the component's properties, one click at a time. Lazur waits for each click. You make each change, and ⌘Z undoes the step if a click goes wrong.

The common mistake is treating the circle as a fix. Lazur shows you where the layer is. It does not change the layer. If your team uses a component library, change the main component, not a copy. For the component steps, see /how-to/create-a-component-in-figma.
Designers and game designers share the same file habits. For HUD, menu and prototype work on a Mac, see /for/game-designers/figma.
Design docs in Notion without typing every line

Design docs are where most of the day ends up. A feature spec, a balance note and a meeting summary all live in Notion. Typing every line by hand takes the afternoon. Hold fn and dictate instead. Clean, formatted text lands at the cursor, in Notion or any other app.

Dictate the rough version first, then edit. Speech tends to be looser than writing, so plan on a pass for wording. Use snippets for text you type each week, such as the header for a systems doc. Add words the speech engine misses to the personal dictionary, like enemy names or ability codes.

Structure still matters. Type / in Notion to insert a block, then ask Lazur to guide you through a layout you have not used before. For a callout box that flags open balance questions, see /how-to/add-a-callout-in-notion. For a database that tracks encounters, see /how-to/create-a-database-in-notion.

Watch for dictation at the wrong cursor. If you hold fn while the cursor sits in a search bar, the words go there. Click into the document, check the cursor, then hold fn. That small check saves a cleanup pass.
Balance spreadsheets: explaining errors and formulas

Balance work lives in spreadsheets. A damage curve, an economy table and a drop rate sheet depend on formulas that break quietly. One error cell can flow into every row below it. Ask what the error means before you click through the formula bar and change things at random.

Hold ⌥ ⌘ while the sheet is open, then ask why one cell shows an error. Lazur reads what is on your screen and explains the cause out loud. It does not rewrite the formula or fill the column for you. Copy the fix yourself, then test it on a few sample rows you can check by hand.

Edge cases matter. Lazur only sees what is on your screen. If the error sits far down the sheet, scroll there first. Long formulas are harder to read in a screenshot, so expand the formula bar before you ask.
For counting values, see /how-to/count-unique-values-in-google-sheets. For drop-down lists in a tuning sheet, see /how-to/create-a-dropdown-list-in-google-sheets.
Slack replies: draft fast, read before you send

A programmer asks why crouch speed changed. A producer wants a status before the end of the day. Each reply takes a few minutes from a blank box. Ask Lazur for a draft instead. Say who you are writing to, what you decided and what you need back.

Read every draft before you send it. Lazur's wording is a starting point, not a message to send unseen. Check the names, the build numbers and the dates. A draft that says a build is ready when it is not costs the team more than a slow reply.

Slack keeps its quick switcher on ⌘K. Use it to jump to the channel. If a thread runs long, hold ⌥ ⌘ and ask what was decided and who owns the fix. That question gets a short answer, and you can paste it into your own reply.
Watch the channel name too. A private note about a teammate can end up in a public channel if you paste into the wrong place. Check the channel header before you send.
Research on how other games handle a mechanic

Research is where a designer checks other games before deciding. Ask Lazur how a few shipped games handle the opening minutes of a tutorial. Research runs in Lazur's own Chrome tabs, which you can open and check. It comes back with a summary and a report.

Treat the summary as a lead, not a citation. Summaries can misread a patch note or a forum post. Open the pages it used before you quote them in a design review. Read the page yourself for any claim that changes a balance decision.
Edge cases: paywalls, login walls and sites that block automated browsing return less. Say so in your request. Ask for the sources used, and ask Lazur to flag any claim it could not confirm.
Confidential design, NDAs and what gets sent

Unreleased design is confidential. Your studio's NDA and AI policy decide what you can show an assistant. Lazur is not a compliance product, and it does not set those rules for you. Follow your employer's rules first, then decide what goes on screen.

Here is what Lazur does with data. It listens and looks at the screen only while you hold the shortcut. Audio and the screenshot go to AI providers to answer you. They are not stored. Content is never used to train AI models. Memory of what you asked stays on the Mac.

Practical rule. Before you hold ⌥ ⌘ on a build with unannounced art, close the window that shows it, or move to a window you can share. If your studio policy is unclear, ask your producer before you use the assistant on that work.
Mistakes game designers make with an AI assistant

items: Trusting a balance number without testing it. Lazur answers from the screen and general knowledge. Check the number in your own build.
Expecting it to click. Lazur points and guides. Your hands do the clicks.
Dictating into the wrong window. Check the cursor before you hold fn.
Sending a draft unread. Read it, fix it, then send it.
Treating research as proof. Open the page for any claim that drives a decision.
Forgetting the shortcut is hold to talk. Keep ⌥ ⌘ held while you ask.

blocks.text: Setup on your Mac and the free trial

Start at /download. Lazur runs on macOS, on Apple silicon and Intel Macs. Windows is planned but not available yet. When you open the app, macOS asks for microphone and screen access. Those two permissions let Lazur hear you and see your screen.

To check your macOS version, open the Apple menu > About This Mac. Compare it with the table above before you install a design tool. A Mac that runs Figma may still be too old for the Unity 6.3 Editor.

The trial has no credit card requirement. It starts when you first open the app. Plans and AI action limits are on /pricing. Dictation is unlimited on the paid plans, so test it on a real design doc before you decide.
A first hour with Lazur

items: Open your HUD file in Figma and hold ⌥ ⌘ to ask where one layer sits.
Open a design doc in Notion and hold fn to dictate one paragraph.
Open a balance sheet and ask why one cell shows an error.
Ask Lazur to draft one Slack reply, then read it before you send it.

faq.question: Does Lazur run inside Figma or Notion?
faq.answer: No. Lazur runs as its own app on your Mac. It is not a plugin or add-in for any app, and it is not affiliated with Figma, Notion, Slack or Unity. It points, explains, guides and drafts. It does not operate the apps for you.

faq.question: Will Lazur move layers or change my Figma file?
faq.answer: No. Lazur does not click buttons, edit files or operate other apps. It can point at a layer, explain a setting or guide you one click at a time. Your hands do the editing, so you stay in control of the file.

faq.question: Does Lazur work on Windows?
faq.answer: Not yet. Lazur runs on macOS, on Apple silicon and Intel Macs. Windows is planned but not available. If your team works on Windows machines, plan your trial on a Mac you can use.

faq.question: Which Mac do I need for Figma and Unity?
faq.answer: The Figma desktop app supports macOS 12 (Monterey) or later on Intel and Apple silicon Macs. Unity 6.3 requires macOS Ventura 13 or newer, and Apple silicon needs an M1 or later. Check your version under the Apple menu > About This Mac before you install.

faq.question: Can I use Lazur with unreleased design documents?
faq.answer: Follow your studio's NDA and AI policy first. Lazur sends audio and the screenshot to AI providers to answer you, and they are not stored. Content is never used to train AI models. Lazur is not a compliance product, so your studio's rules still decide what goes on screen.

faq.question: Does research from Lazur count as a source?
faq.answer: Treat it as a lead. Lazur returns a summary and a report from its own Chrome tabs. Open the pages it cites before you use a claim in a balance review or a design doc. Summaries can misread a patch note or a forum post.

faq.question: Is there a free trial?
faq.answer: Yes. The trial needs no credit card and starts when you first open the app. Plan details and AI action limits are on the pricing page.

faq.question: Will Lazur replace a producer or a level designer?
faq.answer: No. It answers questions and drafts text. Decisions about pacing, balance and scope stay with you and your team. Use it to clear the small tasks that sit between those decisions.

painPoints.title: Messages arrive all day
painPoints.text: Microsoft's Work Trend Index says the average worker receives 117 emails a day and 153 Teams messages a weekday. Each ping pulls attention off the design you are building.

painPoints.title: Interruptions break the thread
painPoints.text: Microsoft also reports interruptions about every two minutes during core hours. A balance thought lost after one ping can be hard to rebuild.

painPoints.title: Work about work
painPoints.text: Asana's 2021 index says knowledge workers spend almost two-thirds of their time on work about work. Status updates and file hunts crowd out the design itself.

painPoints.title: Docs take the afternoon
painPoints.text: Design docs, specs and meeting notes all need typing. Writing them by hand after a long day of tweaking feels slow and error prone.

painPoints.title: Hunting inside big files
painPoints.text: A HUD or menu file can hold many layers. Scrolling the layers panel to find one value is slow and easy to get wrong.
